newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: After coup, Cambodia's royal residences deserted.
newsitem.headline: After coup, Cambodia's royal residences deserted.

text.p: There's no one to protect at the ochre-walled royal palace in Phnom Penh these days.

Bored beige-uniformed guards, shoulders slung casually with ancient assault rifles, sidle away from their posts and pass the time chatting with "motodop" motorcycle taxi drivers, or seek shelter from the sun and occasional monsoon showers beneath nearby trees.
Barriers are out around the palace to stop traffic, but the guards do not prevent motorists driving around them or attempt to check the identity of visitors.

Just over a week after the bloody overthrow of Prince Norodom Ranariddh, King Norodom Sihanouk, who like his son was out of Cambodia when fighting broke out in Phnom Penh, remains in the Chinese capital Beijing, largely aloof from the political fray.
His palace, its gilded spires dominating Phnom Penh's riverfront, is deserted except for a skeleton staff needed for its upkeep, officials there said.
All prominent members of the royal family fled after the fighting on July 5 and 6 between Ranariddh's forces and those of victorious Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, they said.
The palace itself was untouched in the clashes but at Ranariddh's residence, just a few hundred metres (yards) away, it's a very different story.
The scene of some of the heaviest fighting between the rival factions, it still bears the scars.
A large hole in the orange-tiled roof remains from a rocket-propelled grenade, and awnings hang askew.

A smell of burning lingers and piles of debris, including a broken floral lavatory bowl and an empty cognac bottle, remain as evidence of the drunken, indiscriminate looting that followed the fall of the residence.

While barefoot Buddhist monks picked carefully through broken glass littering the pavement, government soldiers said reporters were not allowed to enter the residence. A ministerial bodyguard explained that officials were inside searching for papers signed by the first prime minister.

Hun Sen has sought to justify his overthrow of First Prime Minister Ranariddh by accusing him of infiltrating outlawed Khmer Rouge guerrillas into the city and importing weapons. He has said Ranariddh can return to Phnom Penh but would have to stand trial.
Palace official Gerard Brisse, a Frenchman who is an honorary minister in Sihanouk's cabinet, said he didn't know when the king or other royal family members would return.

"The principal members of the royal family have gone. They have all flown away, to Bangkok or to Singapore," he said. Asked when they might come back, he said: "We have no news. All we can do is ask the astrologers and pray to Buddha."
Among about a dozen senior royals who fled were Ranariddh's son, Prince Norodom Chakravuth, and Sihanouk's favourite daughter, Princess Bopha Devi, a former dancer in the royal ballet.
Brisse said the 74-year-old monarch's return would depend on his health. "He still has some problems with arterial sclerosis and must avoid too much physical activity or stress."

Sihanouk, himself ousted in a coup in 1970, has spent much of his time since his 1993 restoration as monarch in China receiving medical treatment. He has avoided taking sides since his son's overthrow, but called for reconciliation.
Hun Sen has said he has no plan to abolish the monarchy, although he rebuffed Sihanouk's offer to hold reconciliation talks.

Sihanouk said in an interview published in his monthly information bulletin on Sunday that he could not judge whether or not Hun Sen's action amounted to a coup. But by saying he would not sign any decrees or state documents from the government, the king indicated he would not endorse the administration.

Brisse said that as constitutional monarch, Sihanouk was obliged to remain neutral. "He can't take a position in this confrontation between Hun Sen and Ranariddh, but he is trying to avoid new conflict as it is the Cambodian people who suffer.
"The king reigns, but does not rule," he said.
